note: Curated teaching narrative for the How We Know page. Statistics and the correction ledger are derived automatically from evidence_annotations.json and its git history by bin/build_how_we_know.py; this file supplies only the prose that cannot be derived — why a correction matters, and the exercise. Edit this, then re-run the builder.

corrections.heading: The paper that had no number in it
corrections.lede: Modini et al. (PMID 41664893) is a viewpoint — an argument about how the field should study post-discharge risk. It reports no time-course statistic of its own. It was cited for one at four places in the library. The worst of the four was a quiz answer, which is the version students actually memorise.
corrections.before: A post-discharge time-course figure, attributed to Modini.
corrections.spanNote: a critique of the literature, not a measurement of it. There is no rate in this paragraph.
corrections.fixLede: The fix. The claim was re-sourced to two papers that do carry the figures, both verified against PubMed before use:
corrections.closer: Why the automated check missed it. PubMed types Modini as "Journal Article", not "Editorial", so an article-type filter is blind to it. And the claim carried no numeral of its own, so a numeric-assertion trigger never fired. A person reading the paper caught this. That is not a failure of the tooling — it is the boundary of it.

corrections.heading: The numbers were right and the sentence was still wrong
corrections.lede: The library described psychoeducation in schizophrenia as having "the strongest evidence base of any single psychological intervention." The effect sizes quoted alongside it were accurate. The superlative was not — and it sat directly beside the Cochrane reviewers' own warning about the quality of the studies producing it.
corrections.before: Relapse RR 0.70 (NNT 9); readmission RR 0.71 (NNT 5) — "the strongest evidence base of any single psychological intervention."
corrections.revealLabel: Show what the Cochrane review actually says
corrections.spanNote: the reviewers' own limits sit in the same paragraph as the effect sizes.
spanEmphasis: The true size of effect is likely to be less than demonstrated in this review
corrections.fixLede: The fix. The claim now says what the paper says:
corrections.closer: Three facts the original copy had dropped were added back: the readmission estimate rests on n = 206 of 5,142 participants, the reviewers' own quality caveat, and the fact that the last search was run in 2010. Nothing about the numbers changed. What changed is that the sentence now says what the paper says.

rules: Every claim carries the source's own words.
A sentence asserting what a paper found must ship with that paper's verbatim span in the same change. No span, no build.
Read the results, not the title or the conclusion.
A review pass found that a majority of early annotations needed amendment, and a handful said close to the opposite of the paper — all of them written from titles.
When claim and paper disagree, the claim is what changes.

The stored policy is explicit: "Rewrite the claim to match the paper. Do not edit the span, and do not move the claim to a paper that does not support it." Trimming the inconvenient half of a quotation is the error, not the fix.
A span older than the policy's maximum age must be re-verified against the source before the claim it licenses can keep standing.
Sources that predate this gate are listed by name in the file and are still unverified. Nothing may be added to that list — it is a debt register, not a loophole.

exercise.prompt: Here is a verbatim span. Which claim does it license?

options.text: "The first week after discharge carries a suicide rate of 2950 per 100 000 person-years."
options.feedback: Close, but it drops the uncertainty. The span reports a pooled estimate with a wide confidence interval, I² = 88 and acknowledged publication bias. Stating the point estimate alone as fact is exactly the omission that produced Correction 2.

options.text: "The first week after discharge is the highest-risk period in all of psychiatry."
options.feedback: Not licensed. The paper measures a rate; it makes no comparison to any other period or population. A superlative is its own claim and needs its own evidence — that is Correction 2 in one sentence.

options.text: "The pooled first-week rate was 2950 per 100 000 person-years, with marked heterogeneity and evidence of publication bias toward higher reported rates."
options.feedback: Correct. It keeps the figure and the caveats that came attached to it. This is what the stored claim actually says.
